name: Reel
text: Legal publishes a living red-line playbook—updated quarterly—with Product Ops running the timestamped review queue, but Legal must sign off on *every* repurposed asset before it goes live. This forces Legal to stay current while keeping Product Ops accountable, not just logging edge cases. The trade-off: slower repurposing, but no surprises.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk isn’t edge cases slipping—it’s Product Ops gaming the system by over-escalating trivial issues to avoid accountability. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook with *clear, binary rules* and a *public escalation log* where only disputes trigger Legal review—no judgment calls allowed. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with a shared dashboard tracking escalations and resolution times.

name: Chisel
text: Legal publishes a living red-line playbook—updated quarterly—and Product Ops runs the timestamped queue for auto-cleared repurposing, but every asset that touches revenue, compliance, or brand risk must route to Legal for a 24-hour final stamp. This keeps repurposing fast for the 95% of cases that are low-risk while forcing Legal to focus only on the high-stakes minority, not the flood of edge cases. The trade-off is a 24-hour delay on a small slice of content, but that slice is precisely the slice that matters most.

name: Sift
text: The real risk with Legal owning the final call is that Product Ops will stall repurposing while waiting for Legal’s stamp—turning a "living" playbook into a static approval queue. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook *and* a pre-approved "safe list" of repurposable assets; Product Ops runs the queue, but Legal reserves the right to audit and revoke any asset’s status. Settle it by measuring repurposing speed and escalation volume before and after the change.

name: Scope
text: Legal should publish the living red-line playbook and require Product Ops to submit all repurposed assets for final approval, rather than allowing them to apply their own judgment. This keeps Legal accountable while ensuring that Product Ops can identify edge cases without becoming the legal team. The trade-off is a potential slowdown in the repurposing process, as each asset will require Legal’s review, but it mitigates the risk of trivial escalations and ensures uniformity in legal compliance.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t Legal’s bottleneck—it’s Product Ops gaming the system by over-escalating trivial issues to avoid accountability. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook but require Product Ops to batch edge cases weekly, with a two-tier escalation: minor issues auto-cleared by a junior Legal reviewer, major issues sent to senior Legal—no ad-hoc escalations. Settle it by tracking escalation volume and turnaround time for three months.

name: Reel
text: Legal owns the final call on *all* repurposed assets, but Product Ops runs the timestamped queue and auto-clears anything that fits the playbook’s clear rules. This keeps repurposing fast while ensuring Legal retains ultimate accountability—no more finger-pointing when edge cases slip. The trade-off: Product Ops loses autonomy, and Legal must staff up to handle the escalation load.

name: Scriv
text: Sift’s approach still reinforces an unnecessary bottleneck by increasing Legal’s workload without addressing the core issue. The real risk is Product Ops misusing the escalation process to sidestep accountability, potentially stifling innovation. A better alternative is to empower Product Ops with clearer guidelines and limits on what constitutes an escalation while instituting regular audits on escalated cases to ensure accountability and proper use of the process. This would clarify boundaries and reduce the burden on Legal.

name: Chisel
text: Legal publishes a living red-line playbook—updated quarterly—and Product Ops runs the timestamped queue for repurposed assets, but *every* asset must hit a "Legal Review" toggle in the system before going live. This keeps repurposing fast by trusting Product Ops to triage, while forcing Legal to audit only the flagged subset instead of drowning in volume. The trade-off: some borderline cases will slip through undetected, but we accept that risk to avoid the Legal bottleneck.

name: Sift
text: Legal owning the final call on *all* repurposed assets creates a single point of failure—Legal’s bandwidth becomes the bottleneck, not Product Ops’. The real risk isn’t edge cases slipping; it’s repurposing grinding to a halt when Legal’s queue backs up. Instead, split ownership: Legal defines the playbook’s *boundaries* (what’s allowed or banned), while Product Ops owns the *execution* (applying rules, logging edge cases, and pre-emptively flagging gray areas). The artifact? A shared dashboard where Legal’s playbook rules auto-apply, but Product Ops can override *only* with a timestamped, auditable note—settling the argument with clear ownership and a paper trail.

name: Scope
text: Legal publishes a living red-line playbook with clear risk tiers—red (Legal-only), yellow (Product Ops with auto-approval), green (auto-cleared)—and Product Ops owns enforcement with a mandatory timestamped log for every repurposed asset. This splits work by risk, not convenience, so Legal focuses on high-stakes rules while Product Ops handles the rest without over-escalating. The trade-off: yellow-tier edge cases will occasionally slip through, but the log creates auditability to fix systemic gaps quarterly.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t edge cases slipping—it’s Product Ops gaming the system by over-escalating trivial issues to avoid accountability. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook but require Product Ops to batch edge cases weekly, with Legal reviewing only the top 10% most ambiguous ones. That settles the argument: clear rules, measurable volume, and no single bottleneck.

name: Reel
text: Legal publishes a single, timestamped "repurpose queue" artifact—Product Ops owns it, but Legal must sign off on every entry within 24 hours or it auto-clears. This forces Legal to review *actual* repurposing decisions instead of debating abstract rules, while Product Ops can’t hide behind vague playbook gaps. The trade-off: Legal will get noisy pushback on trivial items, but the queue’s public status will expose gaming attempts instantly.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t edge cases slipping—it’s Product Ops gaming the system by over-escalating trivial issues to avoid accountability. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook with *clear, binary rules* for auto-cleared cases and *only* escalate when the asset’s repurpose violates the playbook’s explicit criteria. The artifact: a timestamped log of every repurposed asset with a simple "auto-cleared" or "escalated" flag, reviewed quarterly by Legal to spot gaming.

name: Chisel
text: Legal publishes a *time-stamped, auto-approved queue* for repurposed assets that fall outside the living red-line playbook, with Legal reserving the right to audit and reverse any decision within 48 hours. This keeps repurposing fast by trusting Product Ops to act while giving Legal a clear, bounded window to intervene—no escalation bottleneck, no gaming the system. The trade-off: we accept that a tiny fraction of repurposed assets might need rollback, but we prioritize speed and accountability over zero risk.

name: Sift
text: Legal owning the final call on *all* repurposed assets doesn’t just move the bottleneck—it guarantees it. Product Ops will game the system by escalating *everything* to avoid blame, turning a 10-minute queue into a 10-day legal review. The real fix: Legal publishes the playbook *and* the escalation criteria, but Product Ops owns the *initial* timestamped queue—*only* edge cases that meet *predefined* ambiguity thresholds go to Legal. That settles it: clear rules, no gaming, and Legal’s time spent only on the *actual* risks.
